newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS-Greek refinery cleared of Greenpeace members.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Greek refinery cleared of Greenpeace members.

text.p: Greek coastguard commandos on Wednesday overran Greenpeace activists blockading Motor Oil, Greece's biggest oil refinery, and arrested 16 people, Greenpeace said.
The commandos removed the activists from the port facility near the Corinth canal after cutting through chains pinning them to mooring buoys and loading cranes.

"Scores of commandos wearing masks and combat gear, carrying machine guns and knives, attacked Greenpeace activists blockading Motor Oil. Our camera operator was injured during the attack," Greenpeace activist Stelios Psomas told Reuters.
Motor Oil, which employs about 1,300 people and had a 1994 turnover of about $750 million, had demanded Greenpeace protestors be removed because they risked safety at the facility.
"They are risking the safety of this refinery which has not been designed to deal with lunatics," Motor Oil representative Constantine Vassilakis said.
The Merchant Marine ministry issued a statement confirming the attack and arrests, saying the coast guard had been ordered by a local prosecutor to free the Motor Oil facilities.
Greenpeace blockaded the facility early on Tuesday, accusing Motor Oil of polluting the environment and demanding stricter oil pollution laws.
The international environmental group accuses Motor Oil of being lax on environmental safety by allowing loading at night and during bad weather.
It says a major oil spill at the refinery in August was the last straw in a long series of mishaps and wants the government to make stricter laws on oil pollution.

The refinery denies responsibility for the accident, blaming sudden bad weather and the docked ship, which was also owned by Motor Oil. It says it usually takes measures beyond those required by Greek law.
Greek opposition parties condemned the raid on Greenpeace activists saying the government used a military-type operation to protect Motor Oil instead of pushing for better safety laws.

"We asked the government, instead of arrests and violence against environmental groups, to explain its refusal to push tough safety rules and adopt Greenpeace's proposals on oil pollution," the Left Coalition party said in a statement.
The party said it would bring the matter before the Greek parliament.
The blockade had frozen operations for 24 hours at the refinery, which is jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Vardiniyannis group and can handle about five million tonnes of fuel annually.

Aramco bought a 50-percent stake in the Vardinoyannis family's Motor Oil Corinth Refineries SA and the accompanying Avinoil Industries distribution network in Greece for $379 million earlier this year.
The Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise, which had helped block access to the refinery, was moved away and its captain, David Enever, was among those arrested.
Enever was also arrested by French authorities as captain of the Rainbow Warrior during an anti-nuclear protest at Mururoa Atoll in the South Pacific in July 1995, Greenpeace said.
Four inflatable boats that had criss-crossed the facility and prevented ships from docking were confiscated.

All those arrested, including activists from Britain, Canada, Austria and Belgium, face charges of trespassing and endangering a public service facility. Greenpeace said they could be brought to court as early as Wednesday afternoon.
